newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Record fine for Deutsche UK fund arm.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Record fine for Deutsche UK fund arm.

text.p: Investments watchdog IMRO on Wednesday fined Deutsche Bank's British fund arm a record two million pounds ($3.3 million) for a catalogue of rule breaches and management failings.

The Investment Management Regulatory Organisation also imposed costs of a million pounds on two Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) subsidiaries and lambasted them for not informing the watchdog of concerns.
It said at least one MGAM board member had been informed of problems at the funds, two of which were managed by Peter Young, by April 1996.
Difficulties at three MGAM funds emerged last September when they were temporarily suspended due to serious irregularities in the valuation of unlisted securities.

German parent Deutsche Bank made a cash injection of 180 million pounds into the funds and Young was suspended and later dismissed. Deutsche has since reached a compensation agreement with IMRO for investors disadvantaged by the affair and is expected to pay out around 220 million pounds.

IMRO said it had yet to reach its conclusions about the individuals responsible for the management and supervision of the Morgan Grenfell European Growth Trust, the Morgan Grenfell Europa Fund and the Dublin-based Morgan Grenfell European Capital Growth Fund.

Two of these, the European Growth and the Capital Growth funds, were managed by Young whose activities are under investigation by Britain's Serious Fraud Office. Young has denied any criminal activity.

IMRO chief executive Phillip Thorpe said the mismanagement of the three funds had "caused unnecessary concern to an enormous number of investors". Around 90,000 retail investors had money invested in funds.
In an important footnote to a detailed statement, IMRO said the irregularities were connected with, but not limited to, Young's activities.

It said Morgan Grenfell International Funds Management had not ensured that the managers of the funds were adequately supervised despite concerns about the inappropriate use of investment companies to circumvent regulations, the unusually high proportion of unlisted securities and their repeated failure to provide evidence of due diligence.
IMRO also said there had been repeated attempts by the fund managers "to exploit perceived loopholes in the regulations" as well as other activities that ought to have set alarm bells ringing.

MGAM chief executive Robert Smith, who replaced the previous head Keith Percy in the aftermath of the affair, said that failings in the unit trust business had been addressed and that compliance, controls and operating methods had been subjected to rigorous review.
"I have full confidence in the people and systems we now have in place," he said.
Percy, along with directors Glyn Owen, Graham Kane and Michael Wheatley all left the firm in October following an internal probe into the irregularities found management failings.

IMRO's Thorpe said in the statement that the firm had "paid dearly as a consequence of inadequate management control", adding that the affair illustrated "the dangers of ignoring clear and repeated warnings".
